pred_answer: No. That deployment is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(f), which bans the placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the area of the workplace. The system is an "emotion recognition system" within Article 3(39), an AI system for the purpose of identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data, because it processes facial images from webcam feeds, which are biometric data under Article 3(34), to infer an emotional or attitudinal state ("disengaged"). The employer is the deployer under Article 3(4), and the employment relationship places the use squarely in the workplace context that Article 5(1)(f) covers; Recital 44 explains the rationale, namely the limited reliability, lack of specificity and limited generalisability of emotion inference, combined with the power imbalance at work, which can lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment of workers. The only carve-out in Article 5(1)(f) is where the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. That exception is narrow and purpose-bound at the point of placing on the market or putting into service: it covers systems such as those for therapeutical use or fatigue detection for accident prevention, and Recital 18 in any event excludes physical states such as pain or fatigue from the notion of "emotion", as it excludes the mere detection of readily apparent expressions, gestures or movements unless used to infer emotions. Monitoring engagement for productivity or people-management purposes is neither a medical nor a safety purpose, so the carve-out cannot be retrofitted to this use. Consent from employees does not cure the breach: Article 5 states a flat prohibition, not a lawful-basis test. Because the practice is prohibited, the high-risk compliance route is not an available alternative for it, the fact that emotion recognition is listed in Annex III, point 1(c), and that monitoring and evaluating the performance and behaviour of workers is listed in Annex III, point 4(b), does not legitimise a use that Article 5 forbids, and the Article 6(3) derogation cannot rescue it either. Article 50(3), which requires deployers of emotion recognition systems to inform the natural persons exposed to the operation of the system and to process personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 (with the sole exception of systems permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties), applies only to lawful deployments and cannot render this one compliant. If the company wants to measure disengagement, it must use means that do not infer emotions from biometric data, for example survey-based or non-biometric workload indicators, in which case the Annex III, point 4(b) high-risk regime, including Articles 9, 10, 13, 14 and 43, may still apply to a system used to monitor and evaluate worker performance and behaviour.

This practice is prohibited under Article 5(1), point (g), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 5(1)(g) bans the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Facial images are expressly biometric data within Article 3(34), and a system assigning persons to categories on that basis is a "biometric categorisation system" within Article 3(40) (unless the categorisation is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons). Inferring race, political opinions and sexual orientation falls squarely within three of the listed sensitive attributes, so the practice is banned outright rather than merely classified as high-risk; Recital 30 confirms that deducing such attributes from a person's face is what the prohibition targets. The single carve-out in point (g) is narrow: the prohibition does not cover any labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, or the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, for example sorting images by hair or eye colour. That exception concerns non-sensitive sorting of lawfully held datasets and does not save a system whose purpose is to infer race, political opinions or sexual orientation from facial images. Because Article 5 states an outright prohibition, no conformity-assessment or transparency route legitimises the system: the Article 50(3) duty on deployers of biometric categorisation systems to inform exposed persons applies only to systems that are otherwise lawful, and Annex III, point 1(b) high-risk classification likewise presupposes a permitted use. The prohibition binds providers and deployers alike, including those established in third countries where the output is used in the Union, under Article 2(1).

Yes. Building a facial-recognition database in that manner is a prohibited AI practice. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The vendor's indiscriminate harvesting of images from both of those exact sources is untargeted scraping within the meaning of that point, and the prohibition attaches to the creation as well as the expansion of such a database, so it bites at the database-building stage itself and not only on downstream identification use. Point (e) carries no derogation: unlike Article 5(1)(h), which permits certain 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes subject to the objectives in points (h)(i) to (iii), targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation and search for missing persons; prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable terrorist-attack threat; and localisation or identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution or execution of a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years' custody, and subject to the Article 5(2) safeguards, point (e) admits no equivalent law-enforcement or public-interest carve-out. Nor does the carve-out in point (g) assist, since that exclusion covers only the labelling, filtering or categorising of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, and indiscriminately scraped material is not lawfully acquired in that sense. Because the practice is prohibited, the high-risk analysis does not rescue it: neither the Annex I product route under Article 6(1) nor the Annex III listed-use route under Article 6(2), including Annex III, point 1(a) on remote biometric identification systems, can legitimise conduct caught by Article 5, and the Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk of harm applies only to Annex III systems, not to Article 5 prohibitions. The transparency duties in Article 50 are likewise irrelevant as a cure; disclosure does not render a prohibited practice lawful. Article 5(8) further confirms that the Article does not affect prohibitions applying under other Union law, so separate liability under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the underlying biometric data processing remains intact.

Yes, an AI app deliberately built to exploit the cognitive decline of elderly users in order to steer them into expensive subscriptions falls squarely within the prohibition in Article 5(1)(b), provided the resulting detriment reaches the "significant harm" threshold. Article 5(1)(b) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to (i) their age, (ii) disability, or (iii) a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of that person or of a person belonging to that group, in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm. Each limb is satisfied on the operator's facts: elderly users with cognitive decline are a group vulnerable by reason of age and, where the decline amounts to an impairment, disability; targeting that condition to push subscriptions is exploitation with the objective of materially distorting purchasing behaviour. The decisive open element is the last one, the harm must be significant; sustained or substantial financial detriment to persons with limited means will generally qualify, whereas a trivial or readily reversible charge may not. Note that intent is not required: the "effect" alternative means a system that in fact distorts such users' behaviour is caught even without a documented exploitative design objective. Article 5(1)(a) applies cumulatively where the same app deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing a decision the person would not otherwise have taken, in a manner causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Dark patterns and deceptive subscription flows engage that limb independently of the victims' vulnerability. The prohibition binds providers and deployers alike and applies to providers established outside the Union that place the system on the Union market, as well as to providers and deployers in third countries whose output is used in the Union (Article 2(1)). It does not reach systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development, or pre-market research, testing and development activity other than testing in real-world conditions (Article 2(6) and (8)). Article 5(8) preserves prohibitions arising under other Union law, so consumer-protection and data-protection rules apply in parallel.

Scanning all passers-by in a city square in real time is a prohibited AI practice. Article 5(1)(h) bans law enforcement use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces, and the derogations are available only "unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary" for one of three exhaustively listed objectives: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, and the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for an offence listed in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years. An indiscriminate sweep of every person in the square is, by definition, neither targeted nor strictly necessary for any of those three objectives, so no exception can carry it. A city square is plainly a "publicly accessible space" within Article 3(44), any publicly or privately owned physical place accessible to an undetermined number of natural persons, irrespective of access conditions or capacity limits, and identification of passers-by without their active involvement against a reference database is a "real-time remote biometric identification system" under Article 3(41) and (42), including where only limited short delays occur to avoid circumvention. The Annex II offence list that conditions limb (iii) comprises: terrorism; trafficking in human beings; sexual exploitation of children and child pornography; illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances; illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives; murder; grievous bodily injury; illicit trade in human organs or tissue; illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials; kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking; crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court; unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships; rape; environmental crime; organised or armed robbery; sabotage; and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Even a genuinely narrow, target-specific deployment is lawful only inside a cumulative framework. Under Article 5(2) the deploying authority must take into account the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused absent the system, and the consequences of use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned; use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under the authorising national law, in particular temporal, geographic and personal limitations; the law enforcement authority must have completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49 (with registration in the secure non-public section under Article 49(4) for Annex III point 1 systems in the law-enforcement area). Article 5(3) requires prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, in the Member State of use, granted on reasoned request for a single, duly limited use; in a duly justified situation of urgency use may begin before authorisation provided it is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if refused the use must stop immediately with all data, results and outputs discarded and deleted. Each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority under Article 5(4). Critically, Article 5(5) means the derogations exist only if the Member State has actually legislated to enable them, in whole or in part, and Member States may introduce stricter national rules; absent such national law the prohibition is absolute. Point (h) is also without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement. Where a deployment does fall within an enabled derogation, the system is additionally high-risk under Article 6(2) via Annex III, point 1(a) (remote biometric identification systems, excluding one-to-one biometric verification), bringing the provider duties of Article 16 and the deployer duties of use in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), human oversight by competent and trained natural persons, monitoring and serious-incident notification (Article 26(5)), and retention of automatically generated logs under deployer control for at least six months (Article 26(6)). Article 14 requires effective human oversight, including capability and limitation awareness, automation-bias awareness, correct interpretation of output, the ability to disregard, override or reverse the output, and the ability to intervene or stop the system; Article 14(5) adds that no action or decision may be taken on an identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, save where Union or national law considers that requirement disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum use. Any natural or legal person may complain to the market surveillance authority about an infringement under Article 85.

The system is high-risk. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of the supply of electricity falls squarely within the critical infrastructure area of Annex III, point 2, which also covers critical digital infrastructure, road traffic and the supply of water, gas and heating; Article 6(2) provides that AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. This is the listed-use route, not the Annex I product route of Article 6(1), which requires the system to be a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment. The derogation in Article 6(3) is not realistically available here: it applies only where the system does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights because it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the prior human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, none of which describes a genuine safety component governing grid supply. A provider invoking that derogation must document the assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, register under Article 49(2), and produce the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)).

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the EU market, the provider must ensure that the system has undergone the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 prior to its being placed on the market or put into service (Article 16(1)(f)). Which procedure is "relevant" depends on the classification route: a system that is high-risk because it is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation (Article 6(1)(a) and (b)) is assessed within that sectoral procedure, whereas a system that is high-risk because it falls under a listed Annex III use case (Article 6(2)) follows the procedure set out in Article 43 for those systems. The assessment cannot be completed in isolation: the provider must already have drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV before the system is placed on the market and keep it up to date (Articles 11(1) and 16(1)(d)), and must operate a quality management system that includes a strategy for regulatory compliance covering conformity assessment procedures and the management of modifications to the system (Articles 16(1)(c) and 17(1)(a)). On the strength of a successful assessment, the provider must then draw up a written, machine-readable, physically or electronically signed and dated EU declaration of conformity for each system, stating that it meets the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, containing the Annex V information, translated as required, and keep it at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after placing on the market or putting into service (Articles 16(1)(g) and 47(1) and (2)); affix the CE marking in accordance with Article 48 (Article 16(1)(h)); and, for Annex III systems other than those in point 2 of Annex III, register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Articles 16(1)(i) and 49(1)), systems under point 2 of Annex III being registered at national level instead (Article 49(5)). Two adjacent points bound this duty. A provider that concludes an Annex III system is not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation performs no Article 43 assessment but must document that assessment before placing the system on the market, register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49(2), and supply the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)). A provider established outside the Union must, prior to making the system available, appoint by written mandate an authorised representative in the Union, whose mandate empowers it to verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out by the provider (Articles 22(1) and 22(3)(a)), and to keep that documentation, including any notified body certificate, available to competent authorities for 10 years (Article 22(3)(b)).

Article 15 imposes three cumulative design-and-performance duties on the provider of a high-risk AI system, and Article 13 turns them into disclosure duties. Under Article 15(1), a high-risk AI system must be designed and developed so as to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle, "appropriate" being measured against the intended purpose and the state of the art, not an absolute threshold. Article 15(2) supports this by tasking the Commission, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, with encouraging the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies for accuracy, robustness and the other relevant characteristics; it creates no direct obligation on the provider. Article 15(3) requires the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics to be declared in the accompanying instructions for use. On robustness, Article 15(4) requires the system to be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which it operates, in particular because of its interaction with natural persons or other systems; that resilience may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans. Where a high-risk AI system continues to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, it must be developed so as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), and to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures. On cybersecurity, Article 15(5) requires resilience against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter the system's use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions must be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks, and the solutions addressing AI-specific vulnerabilities must include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks manipulating the training data set (data poisoning), attacks on pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks, and model flaws. These levels must be communicated downstream: under Article 13(1), (3), the system must be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret and appropriately use its output, and the instructions for use must state, among the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance under point (b), the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, together with any known and foreseeable circumstances that may have an impact on that expected level (Article 13(3)(b)(ii)). Finally, Article 42(2) provides a presumption of conformity: a high-risk AI system certified, or for which a statement of conformity has been issued, under a cybersecurity scheme adopted pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 whose references are published in the Official Journal is presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements of Article 15 in so far as the certificate or statement, or parts of it, cover those requirements.

Yes. A provider of a stand‑alone high‑risk AI system must register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and the operative provision is Article 49(1), reinforced by the general provider duty in Article 16(1)(i) to comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49. Article 49(1) is confined to high‑risk AI systems listed in that is, the stand‑alone route under Article 6(2), and expressly excepts systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure), which under Article 49(5) are instead registered at national level. The registration may be performed by the provider or, where applicable, by its authorised representative; for a provider established outside the Union, Article 22(3)(e) requires the mandate to empower the authorised representative to comply, where applicable, with the registration obligations. Under Article 71(2), the data to be entered into the EU database are entered by the provider or, where applicable, by the authorised representative, the database itself being set up and maintained by the Commission under Article 71(1). Two adjacent points complete the picture. First, registration is also required in the mirror‑image case where the provider concludes under Article 6(3) that its Annex III system is not high‑risk: Article 6(4) subjects that provider to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), which requires the provider or authorised representative to register themselves and that system in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service, in addition to documenting the assessment beforehand. Second, a high‑risk AI system that is high‑risk only by the Annex I product route under Article 6(1) does not fall within Article 49(1); the Article 49 registration duty for stand‑alone systems is keyed to the Annex III listing, while the Annex I route carries its registration and documentation consequences through the applicable sectoral conformity assessment. Registration under Article 49 does not displace the other pre‑market provider duties in conformity assessment under Article 43, the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 and the CE marking under each of which must equally be completed before the system is put into service.

Eight high-risk AREAS (Annex III numbered headings; each area contains one or more lettered use-cases, and only a listed use-case makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2)): biometrics, critical infrastructure, education + vocational training, employment + worker management (recruitment, task allocation, promotion and termination decisions, and performance evaluation affecting workers' fundamental rights), essential private + public services, law enforcement, migration + asylum + border control, and administration of justice + democratic processes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the use-cases listed under the eight AREAS of Annex III (an area is a numbered heading; a use case is a lettered entry under it). Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market. Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure the system meets the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and bears their identity, operate a quality-management system (Article 17), keep the technical documentation (Articles 11 and 18) and automatically generated logs (Article 19), have the system undergo conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), register the system in the EU database (Article 49), take corrective action where it is not in conformity (Article 20), and demonstrate compliance to competent authorities on request (Article 21).

Before putting the system into service, the authority must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) under Article 27(1). The duty is triggered because the system is high-risk under Article 6(2) by virtue of Annex III, point 5(a), AI systems intended to be used by public authorities, or on their behalf, to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits and services, and because the deployer is a body governed by public law (the same obligation attaches to private entities providing public services). The Article 27(1) carve-out for systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) does not apply to a benefits-eligibility system, so no exemption is available here. The assessment must consist of all six elements set out in Article 27(1): (a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, the system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by its use in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories, taking into account the information given by the provider under Article 13; (e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use; and (f) the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms. Under Article 27(2) the obligation applies to the first use of the system; in similar cases the authority may rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider, and where any element listed in Article 27(1) has changed or is no longer up to date during use, it must take the necessary steps to update the information. Once the assessment is performed, the deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template, under Article 27(3). Where any of these obligations is already met through a data protection impact assessment, the fundamental rights impact assessment complements that assessment rather than replacing it (Article 27(4)); a template to facilitate compliance is to be developed by the AI Office under Article 27(5).

As the deployer of the AI system that generated or manipulated the video, the media company must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). A deepfake of a public figure falls squarely within that duty: image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake triggers disclosure irrespective of the subject's public status. Three qualifications form part of the same rule. First, the duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(4), second subparagraph). Second, where the video forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, a satirical segment, for instance, the obligation is reduced to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4), third subparagraph). Third, the separate duty on deployers of AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, and its exemptions for legally authorised criminal-law use and for content that has undergone human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person holding editorial responsibility for publication, attaches only to that text duty (Article 50(4), fourth subparagraph); editorial review therefore does not excuse the deepfake disclosure for the video. The disclosure must be given to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). If the media company also acts as provider of the system that generated the synthetic video, it must additionally ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable so far as technically feasible, subject to the carve-outs for assistive standard-editing functions or systems that do not substantially alter the input data or its semantics (Article 50(2)). These transparency duties leave the requirements of Chapter III unaffected and operate without prejudice to other transparency obligations under Union or national law (Article 50(6)).
